title: Who is a true sati
hook: not those who burn on the husband's pyre, but those who live in faithfulness (Suhi Var M3, ang 787)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the burning world, and a prayer for it to be saved by whatever door it can be saved. Your line was by any door.

Some words carry a compliment and a wound at once. Sati is one. Around Guru Amar Das, it could name a faithful, virtuous woman. It could also name a widow who burned on her husband's funeral pyre, a practice found in parts of the society he lived in. A grieving woman could be pushed toward the fire by the very word that honored her. In the Var of Raga Suhi, Guru Amar Das takes that word and changes who it belongs to.
screen: `A COMPLIMENT AND A WOUND.` → `THE FUNERAL PYRE.` → `THE GURU TAKES THE WORD.`

segments.voice: His saloks, paraphrased. One says: they are not called satis who burn themselves with the bodies of the dead. Nanak, they are known as satis who die from the blow of separation. Another: they too are known as satis who live in modesty and contentment, who serve their Lord and rise each morning to remember Him. He doesn't throw the word away. He keeps it, and takes it off the pyre. Faithfulness stops being one terrible moment at a funeral and becomes a whole life: modesty, contentment, service, a morning remembered. And the love being measured isn't only love for a husband. In the language of the Granth, the soul can be the bride, and the Lord the Beloved. So the true sati is anyone, woman or man, whose heart aches at being apart from God and who lives faithfully because of it. Tradition remembers Guru Amar Das speaking against the burning of widows, and the Sikh Gurus honoring the dignity of women in their sangats. Today's text is part of that memory, in the Guru's own words: gentle in tone, firm in meaning. And notice who the salok has in view: a woman in grief. The Guru's answer is: live. Your faithfulness counts in a living life, not in ashes. If grief ever turns toward hurting yourself, please reach out now: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
screen: `NOT THOSE WHO BURN.` · `MODESTY, CONTENTMENT, SERVICE.` · `THE SOUL AS THE BRIDE.` · `LIVE: FAITHFULNESS IN A LIFE.` · then, large: `NOT THE PYRE.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind someone who has lost a husband, a wife or a partner, a grandmother, a neighbor, a friend's mom, and stay with them a while without pity. Notice what their life still holds, the way they keep going, the people they look after, the small faithful things they do, and let one simple gesture toward them come to mind: a call, a visit, a question about the person they lost. If you pray, hold them in Waheguru on each breath out.
Who is a true sati. Not the one who burns on the pyre, says Guru Amar Das, but the one who lives in modesty, contentment and service, and aches to be near the Lord. Today's word.
screen: `WHO IS A TRUE SATI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not the pyre. Faithfulness lives in a whole life, not one moment. Go gently today.

howItsDone: Sikhs cite these saloks of Guru Amar Das from the Var of Raga Suhi in katha and in teaching about the Gurus' stand on the dignity of women and widows, and on the Gurus' rejection of widow burning.

chat.says: I read that sati meant widow burning. Did the Sikh Gurus honor that?
options: No. Guru Amar Das says a true sati lives in modesty and service, not one who burns.
Yes. Guru Amar Das praises the widow who joins her husband's pyre as faithful.
No. He says the word sati belongs only to women who never marry at all.
chat.meaning: In the Suhi ki Var, satis are not those who burn with the dead, but those who live in modesty, contentment and service.
